solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Underground base with accommodation and emergency exits

definitions.text: Underground base with accommodation and emergency exits

blocks.clueFragment: Underground base with accommodation and emergency exits
blocks.note: surface reading: a secret military bunker with living quarters and escape routes, like a Cold War command post

blocks.clueFragment: Underground base with accommodation and emergency exits
blocks.note: setter's reading: the burrow system of a colony of small long-eared animals, with nesting chambers and many bolt-holes for escape

explanation.surface: A spy-film bunker, dug deep, with living quarters and escape hatches.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is wordplay: the whole clue describes a military bunker until you picture rabbits, whose burrows have chambers to live in and extra holes to bolt from.
explanation.definitionFit: A colony's network of burrows is literally an underground home, and rabbits dig several exits so they can flee predators.

clue.text: ‘Playground rugby’ — I finally put sign up

indicators.note: finally points at the end of the following word, so only its closing letter is kept

blocks.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a public playground or park in Britain
RU is the abbreviation for Rugby Union
taken as written
the last letter of 'put'

explanation.surface: A schoolchild finally signs up for a game of rugby in the playground.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Playground rugby' look like a title, but it splits into two abbreviations. A rec (recreation ground) is the British name for a local park or playing field.
explanation.definitionFit: To enlist someone into an army, club or company is to bring them in as a new member, the verb sense here.

clue.text: Married twice, partly reformed bride’s brought in and welled up

indicators.note: only partly reformed means the word is reshaped a little, with just a couple of its letters changing places
something brought in is taken inside, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: the word itself, to be rearranged; the 's is 'is'
M is the abbreviation for married, used twice

explanation.surface: A bride, married twice, is said to be a reformed character and comes over all tearful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partly reformed' is unusual: only the D and E of the word swap, so the rest of it stays in place before the two Ms go in.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquid that wells up rises to the top of a container, so it has filled it to the rim, past tense.

clue.text: Urban? A cruciverbalist might see it!

blocks.note: surface reading: a crossword fan might spot the meaning of 'urban' at a glance
setter's reading: a solver used to hunting hidden words would notice the two letters of 'it' sitting in the middle of the word 'city'

explanation.surface: A puzzled musing on whether a crossword fan would spot a word like 'urban'.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sentence describes a solver's habit: in cITy the pronoun 'it' is buried at the centre, so 'it' is literally the inner part of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban describes town and metropolitan areas; the hyphenated adjective names the dense central districts of a large town.

clue.text: Legendary golfer‘s clubs

blocks.note: first meaning: Tiger, the American champion with fifteen major titles
second meaning: golf clubs with large heads used for long shots, traditionally made of timber

explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive, the champion's own equipment, but it is just 'is' joining two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Tiger, the famous golfer, is also the name for long-distance golf clubs once made of persimmon timber.

clue.text: One’s getting on, and over wearing formal work gear

definitions.text: One’s getting on, and over wearing formal work gear

indicators.note: whatever is worn is round the wearer, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: re means on or concerning, as in a memo heading
a neckwear item for formal office dress
over in the sense of about, as in a row over money

explanation.surface: An older worker, finished with the job, no longer has to wear a suit and tie to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The same short word answers both 'on' and 'over', both in the sense of 'about'. Read whole, the clue describes someone old enough to be done with office wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has stopped working, usually in later life, is getting on in years and is past wearing office attire.

clue.text: Tesla, say, I’d parked before time, keeping small space clear

indicators.note: coming before means placed earlier in line, so the pieces join in this order
to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a Tesla is an example of an electric vehicle, abbreviated EV
taken as written, without the apostrophe
T is the abbreviation for time
an en is a printer's unit of space, half an em

explanation.surface: A driver explains leaving an electric car parked with a bit of room around it.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a typesetting measure, the width of a narrow space; crossword setters use it, with em, for 'space'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obvious or plain to see is apparent to everyone, the adjective sense of the word.

clue.text: Taking off in limited space? Or limited space for taking off

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: undressing on the small area at the top of a staircase
second meaning: a narrow runway from which light aircraft depart

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves use the same words in different senses: 'taking off' is removing clothes, then leaving the ground; the 'limited space' is a stairhead, then a short runway.
explanation.definitionFit: A short, basic runway for small planes is the restricted ground they use to get airborne; read as two words it is a striptease at the stairhead.

clue.text: Selling point of suit incorporating uniform

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body of something, so one part is held inside

blocks.note: a legal suit is a court case or lawsuit
Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U

explanation.surface: A tailor's sales pitch: the uniform-style cut of a suit is its big attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Selling point' wants to mean an attractive feature; here it is a place or occasion where goods are sold. 'Suit' is legal, not clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A public sale where goods go to the highest bidder is an event or venue for selling, the literal sense.

clue.text: Bird — duck — rolling across street

indicators.note: lying across something means spanning it, so one piece stretches around the other

blocks.note: a duck is a score of zero in cricket, written as O
rolling in it means wealthy
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A comic scene: a bird, a duck, rolling over as it crosses a road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a second bird but is cricket's nought. 'Rolling' looks like a verb but is slang for wealthy, as in 'rolling in money'.
explanation.definitionFit: The large flightless African runner is the biggest living species of bird.

clue.text: One sunbathing, maybe big hit covering nothing on top

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed after the item above it, so these two join in sequence
to cover something is to go all round it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a haymaker is a wild swinging punch
O looks like zero
a lid is the top of a container

explanation.surface: A sunbather on the beach, maybe a big hit, wearing nothing on top.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at topless sunbathing, but 'nothing on top' is O followed by a lid, and that pair goes inside the punch.
explanation.definitionFit: A tourist on vacation is a typical example of a person lying in the sun, hence the 'maybe'.

clue.text: Harem murder implicates backing musician

indicators.note: to implicate is to fold or involve something within, so the letters lie inside the phrase
going backwards means reading from right to left

blocks.note: the letters inside the phrase, read as printed

explanation.surface: A sultan's palace killing points the finger at a member of the backing band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing musician' wants to read as a backing-band player; 'backing' belongs to the wordplay and 'musician' alone is the definition. Read haREM MURDer from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A percussionist who plays a kit of skins and cymbals is one kind of musician.

clue.text: Kind of painting breaking RA rules?

definitions.note: adjective describing a style, as in 'surreal painting'

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, and its letters can be put back in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A style of art that flouts the rules of the Royal Academy.
explanation.walkthrough: The RA is the Royal Academy of Arts in London; dreamlike art of the Dalí school would indeed break its traditional rules.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes dreamlike, bizarre imagery in the manner of the 1920s movement led by Breton and Dalí, a style of art.

clue.text: Written without Sheeran?

blocks.note: without in the sense of lacking or not having
the first name of the English pop singer Ed Sheeran

explanation.surface: Was this song written without Ed Sheeran's help?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful step from a surname to its owner's first name: Ed Sheeran is a hugely successful English singer-songwriter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something jotted down on paper has been recorded in writing, the past participle sense.

clue.text: What’s disturbed DC — Epstein under investigation

definitions.note: phrase used adjectivally; the answer is a past participle

indicators.note: something disturbed has been knocked out of its settled order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Washington is rattled while the Epstein affair is being investigated.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a news headline about Washington and the Epstein files; DC here is just two letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Something examined closely by officials has been scrutinised, which is what being looked into or probed amounts to.

clue.text: Sitting in position around study, heading off change

indicators.note: going around something means enclosing it on both sides
with its head taken off, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: to set is to put in position
a den is a private room for work or study
to vary is to change; drop its first letter

explanation.surface: A seated person in some post, ringing round the office to stop a change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sitting in position' reads as a single phrase, but only 'Sitting' is the definition and 'in' is a link. 'Change' must become VARY before it loses its head.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a lifestyle or job spent mostly seated, involving little physical movement.

clue.text: Higher than natural, I had sung like a hawk?

indicators.note: singing uses the voice, so what matters is how the words come out of the mouth, not their spelling

blocks.note: in music a sharp note is a semitone above the natural
the contraction of 'I had' when spoken

explanation.surface: A singer confesses to being pitched too high, with a voice like a hawk's screech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural' is a musical term here, not 'normal': a note raised from its natural is sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawks are famed for keen vision, so having eyes like a hawk means being observant and quick to spot things.

clue.text: Quick, everyone! Ogre’s on the move

indicators.note: things on the move shift about and settle in a fresh order

blocks.note: everyone means all
the word to be rearranged; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A panicked warning to run because a monster is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' reads as a shout to hurry, but it is the definition, an adjective describing tempo.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction means at a brisk, lively tempo, so a fast passage is marked this way.

clue.text: Ring about working out King’s speech, which should be inspiring

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is placed round another

blocks.note: a peal is the ringing of bells
PT is physical training, exercise
K is the chess abbreviation for king; the 's is 'has' or 'is'

explanation.surface: A boxer's ring and workout lead to the King's address, which ought to inspire, perhaps evoking the film The King's Speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King's speech' looks like a unit, nodding to the film about George VI, but the King gives only one letter and 'speech' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A short rousing address given to motivate a team or group is a speech meant to raise spirits.

clue.text: Welsh town has limited double parking for one in seven workers

indicators.note: to have something limited is to hold it within bounds, so a piece is enclosed

blocks.note: Hay-on-Wye, the book town on the River Wye, known simply as Hay
P for parking, twice

explanation.surface: A Welsh town restricts double parking, a nuisance caused by commuters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seven workers' are the Seven Dwarfs of Snow White, who work in a mine; one of them is named for being cheerful. Hay-on-Wye is a small Welsh town famous for its book festival.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheerful member of Snow White's seven mining dwarfs is one of the band of workers.

clue.text: On drugs, initially thrown inside for year, one’s served around four

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the opening letter is kept
the inside of a word is its middle, without the outer letters

blocks.note: intoxicated, in slang
the first letter of 'thrown'
the middle two letters of 'year'

explanation.surface: A drug user thrown inside for a year, serving a sentence of about four.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a prison story: 'thrown inside' and 'served' suggest jail, but 'inside' picks the middle letters and 'served' belongs to the meal. In Britain this early evening meal comes with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: This late-afternoon British meal of cooked food, bread and cakes with tea is eaten around four or later.

clue.text: Studies Greek hero with more northern university

indicators.note: in a down entry north is upward, so a letter moved further north slots in higher up the column

blocks.note: the slayer of Medusa in Greek myth
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A student reads up on a Greek hero at a university in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: The hero's name already holds U; lift it two places up the column and the name becomes the answer. 'Northern university' looks like a place but is a direction for that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To read something carefully and thoroughly is to examine it closely; third person singular, matching the verb in the clue.

clue.text: Sees pale, raw looking behind, showing evidence of this?

definitions.text: Sees pale, raw looking behind, showing evidence of this?

indicators.note: showing means on display, so the letters are visible within the words
looking behind means facing backwards, so read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters inside the phrase, read as printed

explanation.surface: Someone sees a pale, sore-looking patient behind them, a sign the illness has returned.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a patient looking pale and raw is evidence of falling ill again.
explanation.definitionFit: A return of illness after apparent recovery would show up as a pallid, unwell look, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Appearance of jeans oddly out of place on judge

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are taken away, so only every other letter remains

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of 'jeans'
to try a case is to judge it in court

explanation.surface: A judge turns up in jeans, which looks oddly out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' in a down clue puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Making an entrance onto a stage or into a room is appearing there, the noun sense of arrival.

clue.text: West-facing state perhaps in Commonwealth country

indicators.note: facing west in an across entry means pointing leftward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to air a view is to state it
eg, for example, signals a possibility
taken as written

explanation.surface: A westward-looking state within a Commonwealth nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' wants to be a region of the country, and the answer does have states, but here it is the verb, as in 'air your views'.
explanation.definitionFit: The West African nation joined the association of former British territories on independence in 1960 and remains a member.

clue.text: Leaf set down by insect procession

indicators.note: laid down next to something means placed alongside it in order

blocks.note: a leaf of a book is a page
a common small insect

explanation.surface: A leaf put down beside a line of ants on the march.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaf' suggests a tree, but it is a sheet of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A colourful public parade or show of costumed figures moving through the streets is a type of procession.

clue.text: Dali, for instance — Spain’s entertainer

blocks.note: Salvador Dalí was a painter
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: Dalí, the flamboyant showman, was Spain's great entertainer.
explanation.walkthrough: E is the international car registration letter for Spain (España), a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word names a professional performer such as a singer or dancer, a stage entertainer.

clue.text: Bottom’s adornment enthrals Fairyland’s central character for ages

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece is held within the other
the central character of a word is the single letter at its exact middle

blocks.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream, Puck gives the weaver Bottom an ass's head with long ears
the fifth of nine letters in 'Fairyland'

explanation.surface: Bottom's comic ass's head captivates Titania, queen of Fairyland, for a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' is not a backside but the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, whose transformed head charms the Fairy Queen. Donkey's years is British slang for a very long time.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal idiom means an extremely long time, so it can stand in for 'for ages' after a verb, as in 'not seen him in years'.
